content: A 12-year study in Sri Lanka links declining numbers of wild female Asian elephants to abrupt social fractures that may be difficult to repair. Asian elephants rely on one another to find food, acquire information, and care for young. Keeping that support network intact requires opportunities to build new relationships as old connections are lost. In Sri Lanka’s Udawalawe National Park, a shrinking population appears to be straining that social system. An analysis of more than 440 wild female Asian elephants over 12 years found that large, densely connected communities had given way to smaller, more isolated groups. The remaining females were changing their relationships with one another as their numbers fell. “We see individual elephants leaving and possibly dying at accelerating rates, but new individuals are not coming into the population,” said Anastasia Madsen, the postdoctoral researcher who led the study. “With fewer individuals in the population, those who are left will naturally have fewer relationships. However, the remaining elephants are also changing their relationships with each other.” Published November 12 in Science , the research comes from the University of California San Diego’s School of Biological Sciences. Madsen works in Associate Professor Shermin de Silva’s laboratory in the Department of Ecology, Behavior and Evolution. The analysis points to a combination of likely deaths, elephants leaving permanently, and fewer incoming individuals as explanations for the population decline. Poaching and conflicts with humans already cause deaths in many elephant populations. Disrupted connections between habitats and reduced food availability may also contribute as ecological conditions change across the 119-square-mile park and its surroundings, though these remain possible pressures rather than established causes of the social changes observed here. The researchers interpret the shift in community structure as evidence that the population may have crossed a critical threshold, or social tipping point. “We found that gradual accumulation of losses from turnover preceded sudden change in the social networks among females in a wild population of Asian elephants,” the researchers explained in the study. That sequence raises the possibility that losses can build for years before the organization of an animal society changes abruptly. The resulting fragmentation could be difficult to repair. “In general, we need to be more aware of these types of tipping points where we see sudden shifts after changes have been slowly building up,” said Madsen. “Once we move past the tipping point, it’s much harder to go back to previous states.” The findings add to discussions about conserving elephant populations as people expand into areas where the animals historically thrived. For social species, opportunities to share space and develop relationships are part of what sustains a community. “We can probably all relate to the feeling of social isolation brought about, paradoxically, with the advent of digital communications that seem to remove the physical constraints of needing to be in the same place at the same time,” said de Silva, who also serves as president and founder of the conservation nonprofit Trunks & Leaves Inc.. “But for many social species, which includes ourselves as much as elephants, we have to remember that social connectivity is very much a matter of sharing space and building relationships throughout our lives. Crucially, in order to have resilient communities, we need to be able to replace the relationships that are lost over time.” Future studies can use the findings to investigate how animal societies change, how to detect those shifts, and which factors make communities vulnerable. “We are gaining more evidence that studying social patterns is an important tool for us to see when things are going wrong in natural populations and, hopefully, to be able to do something about it,” said Madsen. Reference: “Increased demographic turnover and isolation precede social fragmentation in Asian elephants” by Anastasia E. Madsen, T. V. Pushpakumara, U. Sameera Weerathunga, Devaka K. Weerakoon and Shermin de Silva, 12 November 2026, Science . DOI: 10.1126/science.aef6714 Funding: US Fish and Wildlife Asian Elephant Conservation Grant F11AP00258 (S.d.S.); US Fish and Wildlife Asian Elephant Conservation Grant F14AP00256 (S.d.S.); US Fish and Wildlife Asian Elephant Conservation Grant F17AP00308 (S.d.S.); International Elephant Foundation; National Science Foundation DBI-2305860 (A.E.M.); University of Pennsylvania; University of California, San Diego; Trunks & Leaves Inc. title: Anthropic’s Wall Street whisperer: Meet CFO Krishna Rao
content: It's been a busy year for Anthropic CFO Krishna Rao . After closing a $65 billion funding round in May, he's been readying the artificial intelligence company for what's widely expected to be a blockbuster initial public offering . The listing could value Anthropic at roughly $1.4 trillion , instantly making it one of the largest tech companies in the world. Rao joined Anthropic in 2024, when the company was still considered an underdog to OpenAI , now its chief rival. He's known as a straight shooter and a deft operator with a relentless work ethic, according to Anthropic investors and former colleagues, and he's played a crucial role in fueling the company's historic rise. The 43-year-old finance chief has largely stayed out of the public eye, opting to yield the spotlight to Anthropic's seven co-founders , including CEO Dario Amodei and President Daniela Amodei . But Anthropic's upcoming Nasdaq debut, which is expected to take place on Thursday, will likely push him to center stage, as public market investors and analysts hang on his every word for insight into the AI trade. Rao has nearly two decades of experience in finance across a range of companies, including Fanatics Commerce, a sports merchandise retailer, Cedar, a healthcare payments and billing platform, Airbnb and Blackstone . But he's never taken a company public as a CFO, and the stakes are high. Investors are still reeling after Jensen Huang resigned as CEO of Nvidia following shocking reports of three extramarital affairs . The market was already jittery on concerns that rising interest rates would make debt unaffordable for companies that need it for costly infrastructure purchases. Against that backdrop, Rao is under pressure to deliver. "He's a committed professional. He's integrity-based, and he's had this meteoric rise in a very, very complex set of companies," Jonathan Mildenhall, Airbnb's former marketing chief and a Fanatics board member, told CNBC in an interview. "There was nothing easy about Airbnb. There was nothing easy about Fanatics. There's nothing easy about Anthropic, and yet he makes it look so." CNBC spoke to current Anthropic investors, Rao's friends and former colleagues for this story, many of whom asked not to be named because they were not authorized to speak publicly. Rao declined to participate in an interview through an Anthropic spokesperson. As Anthropic's first CFO, Rao has been instrumental in helping the company raise tens of billions of dollars over the past two years. He has made himself easily accessible to Anthropic's backers, even during fast-moving, tense discussions about allocation sizes and valuations, according to investors. He often communicates in short bursts of texts or via quick phone calls, sometimes late into the night and through weekends. "He will communicate even bad news very directly, and I think that's important in this role, especially as they're launching into the public life," Byron Deeter , a partner at Bessemer Venture Partners, a repeat Anthropic investor, told CNBC in an interview. "He doesn't let the important stuff go unsaid, and he's very good at giving you headlights into what's coming." Rao has a deep mastery of the nuts and bolts of Anthropic's business, as well as its broader strategy, and he's able to translate the complexities into language that financiers understand, according to investors and a former colleague. That's been especially useful ahead of the IPO, while Wall Street has been working to digest Anthropic's ambitious infrastructure plans , the people said. Anthropic has to secure massive amounts of computing power to train AI models and serve customers, and has entered into a range of purchase and lease agreements to try to meet anticipated demand. The company said in an amended prospectus last week that its aggregate spend commitments total roughly $900 billion, "substantially all of which is related to compute and infrastructure." "The compute that we procure, it's the lifeblood of our business," Rao said during a rare podcast appearance on "Invest Like The Best" in May. "It is the most important thing in the company. It's like the canvas on which everything else gets built." Rao's frank communication style is different from that of Amodei, Anthropic's chief executive, who's known for penning long essays and opining about AI's transformative potential and grave risks. But the pair complement one another well, according to investors, and Rao has earned Amodei's trust. Both executives have been closely involved with Anthropic's fundraising efforts and IPO planning, but Rao has taken the lead in many of those discussions. He's been front and center during Anthropic's road show, and he led the early testing-the-waters meetings that the company held in August, as CNBC previously reported . Deeter called Rao "the glue" of the company, helping turn the founders' ideas into reality. For friends and early colleagues, Rao's ascension hardly came as a surprise. He earned his undergraduate degree in economics at Harvard University, where he graduated summa cum laude in 2005. Six years later, after a stint as a strategy consultant at Bain & Company, he completed his J.D. at Yale Law School. Instead of pursuing a career as a lawyer, Rao took a job at Blackstone and worked as a private equity investor. He soaked up the training he received there and was regarded as a competent and personable teammate, according to a former colleague. Rao is also credited with inspiring the private equity unit's annual poker tournament, after he famously schooled his bosses during a game in 2014. The following year, Rao followed Blackstone's then CFO, Laurence Tosi , to Airbnb, where he cut his teeth in the world of fast-growing tech startups. Rao helped lead the financing that kept Airbnb afloat during the Covid-19 pandemic, which he's publicly described as a "harrowing time" for the business. During his May podcast appearance, Rao said Airbnb lost 70% of its revenue during a seven-week period. The company survived, and Rao helped support its IPO in late 2020 . "Airbnb was so dynamic," said Mildenhall, who is now the chief marketing officer at Rocket Companies . "I think that both his short time at Fanatics and his time at Airbnb really gave him close proximity to visionary founders that have a relentless frustration with the status quo." While Airbnb was one of the fastest-moving startups of the 2010s, it would be dwarfed by the hypergrowth that Rao would later be tasked with steering at Anthropic. Anthropic reported $33.24 billion in revenue for the nine months ending Sept. 30, up roughly 1,200% from the same period last year. In 2024, the year that Rao joined the company, Anthropic generated a total of $386 million in revenue. The company could net more than $60 billion in proceeds through its IPO this week, as CNBC previously reported , and Rao will be charged with deploying that capital and ushering Anthropic into its next phase of life as a public company. As he prepares to dive headfirst into the world of quarterly earnings calls, investors and former colleagues said they believe he's up to the task. "What I do try to do, maybe once a week, is in a quiet moment, just think, 'Wow, this is really cool,'" Rao said in May. "'It's an incredible opportunity to work with this group of people on this problem at this company at this moment in time.'" WATCH: Anthropic’s breakneck rise: What to know before the IPO

The CFO's role in preparing the company for this massive listing and the potential market impact of his words provide a clear reason for readers to care.
